title: Reporting a survival analysis
text: A survival analysis can only be judged if the reader knows how the times were defined and how much information lies behind each number. Reporting guidelines exist for observational studies in general (STROBE, Elm et al. (2007)), for prognostic marker studies (REMARK, McShane et al. (2005)) and for prediction models (TRIPOD, Collins et al. (2015)). The checklist below covers what they ask for in the analyses of this tutorial.

title: Reporting a survival analysis
text:
Checklist
Methods

The time origin and the event, defined precisely (for example “overall survival: time from diagnosis to death from any cause”).
How and when patients were censored (alive at the last contact, end of the study), and the date of closing the follow-up.
The candidate variables, how continuous variables were entered (per unit, per 10 years …), the reference level of each factor, and how variables were chosen for the multivariable model.
How missing data were handled (the module uses complete cases).
The methods: Kaplan-Meier with log-transformed confidence intervals, log-rank test (and trend test for ordered groups), Cox regression, how proportional hazards were checked.
The software and versions.

Results

Number of patients, number of events, and the median follow-up (reverse Kaplan-Meier).
Median survival and survival at clinically relevant times, each with a 95% CI.
The test comparing groups, with its statistic, df and p-value.
Hazard ratios with 95% CI, univariable and multivariable, with the number of patients and events in the model.
The result of the proportional-hazards check.
For interactions: the interaction test, and HRs within subgroups only if it supports them.

Figures

Kaplan-Meier curves with the number at risk under the time axis, the y-axis from 0 to 1 (or 0–100%), and follow-up cut where few patients remain (Pocock et al. 2002; Morris et al. 2019).
Confidence bands, or CIs at key times, so that the reader sees the uncertainty.

title: Reporting a survival analysis
text:
A template
The following paragraphs report the worked examples of this tutorial. Numbers come from the module; replace the software versions with yours (jamovi shows its own version under About jamovi, and the module’s version in the jamovi library of installed modules).

Statistical analysis. Overall survival was defined as the time from enrolment to death from any cause; patients alive at the last contact were censored. Survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method, with 95% confidence intervals computed on the log scale, and follow-up was summarised with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Survival was compared between ECOG performance status groups with the log-rank test and the log-rank test for trend. Hazard ratios (HR) were estimated with Cox proportional hazards regression, univariable and adjusted for sex, age (per 10 years) and ECOG performance status (reference: ECOG 0); the proportional hazards assumption was assessed with scaled Schoenfeld residuals (Grambsch and Therneau 1994). Analyses used jamovi (version …) with the prognosis module (version 0.1.1), which uses the R package survival (Therneau 2026).


Results. Of 226 patients, 163 died during a median follow-up of 19.3 months. Median survival was 12.9, 10.1 and 6.5 months for ECOG 0, 1 and 2, and 1-year survival 54%, 43% and 21% (log-rank p < 0.001; trend p < 0.001). In the multivariable Cox model (Table 2), ECOG 1 and 2 were associated with higher mortality than ECOG 0 (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.02–2.23, and 2.47, 95% CI 1.58–3.86), and women had lower mortality than men (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.81). The crude association of age (HR per 10 years 1.20, 95% CI 1.00–1.44) weakened after adjustment (HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.93–1.34). There was no evidence against proportional hazards (global test p = 0.288).

title: Reporting a survival analysis
text:
Common mistakes

No number at risk under a Kaplan-Meier plot, or curves drawn to the last patient, where the steps are huge and the estimates meaningless.
“Median survival not reached” reported as a number, or survival at a time beyond the follow-up.
Only p-values, no hazard ratios or survival probabilities with CIs.
Univariable screening (“variables with p < 0.05 entered the multivariable model”) without saying so; it biases the results and should be justified.
Too many variables for the number of events.
Subgroup claims without an interaction test (see the subgroup fallacy).
Hazard ratios described as risks: “a 42% lower risk of death” for HR = 0.58 is common but loose; “a 42% lower hazard (rate) of death” is correct.
Censoring the wrong patients: for overall survival, deaths from any cause are events, not censored observations.

title: Time-to-event data and censoring
text:
Every time-to-event analysis starts by fixing three things, and a paper that does not state them clearly cannot be interpreted:

The time origin: when the clock starts. Diagnosis, surgery, randomisation, start of treatment. It should be a moment that is defined in the same way for every patient.
The event: what stops the clock. Death from any cause (overall survival), relapse or death (disease-free or progression-free survival), graft failure, hospital discharge.
The time scale and unit: days, months or years since the origin.

For each patient we then observe a pair \((t_i, \delta_i)\): the time \(t_i\) from the origin to the end of observation, and an indicator \(\delta_i\) that says whether observation ended because the event happened (\(\delta_i = 1\)) or for some other reason (\(\delta_i = 0\)). In the teaching dataset these are the columns time (months) and event (dead or alive).

title: Time-to-event data and censoring
text:
Censoring
A patient whose observation ends before the event is censored. Their survival time is not missing: we know it is longer than \(t_i\). This is called right censoring, because the true time lies somewhere to the right of what we saw. It happens for ordinary reasons:

the study ends (administrative censoring): patients recruited late have been followed for a short time only;
loss to follow-up: the patient moves away or stops attending;
withdrawal, or an event that makes further observation impossible.






















Figure 1: Eight hypothetical patients. Left: they enter a study at different dates and the study closes at month 15 (dashed line). Right: the same patients with each clock started at entry, which is how survival data are analysed. Dots are deaths; crosses are censored follow-up (patient 6 was lost to follow-up, the others were alive when the study closed).



The key assumption of every method in this tutorial is non-informative censoring: patients who are censored at a given time must have the same prospects as those who remain under observation. Administrative censoring is usually harmless. Loss to follow-up may not be: if the sickest patients stop coming to the clinic, the patients who remain look healthier than the cohort really is, and survival is overestimated. No statistical method can repair this. Keep loss to follow-up low and report how much there was.

text:
Why the usual methods fail
Suppose you want the typical survival of the 226 patients. Some obvious shortcuts all give the wrong answer:

Treating a censored time as if the patient had died underestimates survival: the patient lived longer. Dropping censored patients also underestimates it, because the patients still alive at the end of the study are often the long survivors. And the proportion who died, 163/226 = 72%, is not a probability of anything: it depends on how long each patient happened to be followed. A t-test or a linear regression of time has the same problems. Logistic regression of “dead at 12 months” works only for patients followed for at least 12 months and ignores when the deaths happened.
Survival methods use each patient for exactly as long as they were observed, and no longer.

title: Time-to-event data and censoring
section: Three ways to describe the same survival
text:
Three ways to describe the same survival

The survival function \(S(t)\)
\[S(t) = P(T > t)\]
is the probability of being event-free beyond time \(t\). It starts at \(S(0) = 1\) and can only go down. “Two-year survival is 12 %” is a statement about \(S(24 \text{ months})\). The median survival is the time at which \(S(t)\) falls to 0.5. The Kaplan-Meier curve is an estimate of \(S(t)\).


The hazard \(h(t)\)
The hazard is the rate at which events happen at time \(t\) among the patients who are still event-free just before \(t\):
\[h(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{P(t \le T < t + \Delta t \mid T \ge t)}{\Delta t}\]
Think of it as the death rate of the patients still alive at that moment, for example “3% per month at month 6”. The hazard can rise, fall or stay constant over time, and its shape tells a clinical story (Figure 2): the risk after surgery is highest in the first days, the risk of death with age increases, and the risk of a chronic disease may be constant.





















Figure 2: Three hazard shapes (left) and the survival curves they produce (right). A constant hazard of 5% per month gives the exponential curve \(S(t) = e^{-0.05t}\). A decreasing hazard makes the curve drop fast early and then flatten; an increasing hazard does the opposite.



A hazard is a rate, not a probability, so it has a unit (per month, per year) and can be larger than 1. The ratio of two hazards, the hazard ratio (HR), has no unit; it is what Cox regression estimates.


The cumulative hazard \(H(t)\)
\[H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du, \qquad S(t) = e^{-H(t)}\]
adds the hazard up over time. With a constant hazard \(h\), \(H(t) = h\,t\). \(H(t)\) can be read roughly as the expected number of events a patient would have had by time \(t\) if the event could repeat.






TipWhat to remember




\(S(t)\), \(h(t)\) and \(H(t)\) are three descriptions of the same thing: know one and you know the others. If two groups differ in one, they differ in all three.
\(S(t)\) is the easiest to explain to patients. Hazards are what the models work with.
The Kaplan-Meier module draws four views of the same estimate: \(S(t)\), the cumulative incidence \(1 - S(t)\), the cumulative hazard \(H(t)\), and \(\log(-\log S(t)) = \log H(t)\).

title: Comparing curves: the log-rank test
text: Two Kaplan-Meier curves differ in a sample. Is the difference larger than chance would produce if the two groups really had the same survival? We cannot compare mean survival times (censoring), and comparing survival at one chosen time wastes most of the data. The log-rank test (Mantel 1966; Peto and Peto 1972) uses the whole curve with a simple idea: at every time a death happens, compare the number of deaths in each group with the number we would expect if the groups did not differ.

title: Comparing curves: the log-rank test
text:
Observed and expected deaths
Take one event time \(t_j\). Just before it, \(n_{Aj}\) patients of group A and \(n_{Bj}\) of group B are at risk (\(n_j\) in total), and \(d_j\) of them die. If the groups had the same hazard, each patient at risk would be equally likely to be one of the deaths, so group A would expect a share of the deaths proportional to its share of the risk set:
\[E_{Aj} = d_j \,\frac{n_{Aj}}{n_j}\]
This is a 2×2 table (group × died or not) at each event time. Adding up over all event times gives the observed deaths \(O_A = \sum_j d_{Aj}\) and the expected deaths \(E_A = \sum_j E_{Aj}\). The variance of \(O_A - E_A\) also adds up, with a contribution from each table:
\[V_j = \frac{n_{Aj}\, n_{Bj}\, d_j\,(n_j - d_j)}{n_j^2\,(n_j - 1)}, \qquad
  \chi^2 = \frac{(O_A - E_A)^2}{\sum_j V_j}\]
Under the null hypothesis of equal survival, \(\chi^2\) follows a chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

title: Comparing curves: the log-rank test
section: The trend test for ordered groups
text:
The trend test for ordered groups
ECOG 0, 1 and 2 are ordered. The 2-df log-rank test asks whether the three curves differ in any way; the log-rank test for trend gives the groups scores 1, 2, 3 and asks the narrower question, on 1 df, whether survival changes steadily along the order. When the ordering is real, the trend test is more powerful and the conclusion is clearer: “survival worsened with each step of ECOG”. Report it alongside the overall test for ordinal groups (tick Log-rank trend (ordered groups)); it makes no sense for unordered groups such as treatment arms.

title: Comparing curves: the log-rank test
section: What the tests do not tell you
text:
What the tests do not tell you

How large the difference is. The p-value depends on the sample size. For the size of the effect, look at the medians, the survival at fixed times, or a hazard ratio from Cox regression.
Which groups differ, when there are more than two.
Whether the difference is due to the grouping variable itself or to something that goes with it (older patients may have a worse ECOG). Adjustment needs a regression model.

title: Interactions: does one effect depend on another?
text:
Good practice

Decide on interactions before seeing the data, from a clinical question; every extra interaction tested is another chance of a false positive.
Report the interaction test, not only the subgroup results.
Expect low power. Detecting an interaction as large as the main effect needs about four times the sample size (Brookes et al. 2004). A non-significant interaction test means “no evidence of a difference”, not “the effects are equal”.

Step 6: write it up

In a Cox model including sex, age and ECOG performance status (226 patients, 163 deaths), survival was worse with higher ECOG: HR 1.51 (95% CI 1.02–2.23) for ECOG 1 and 2.47 (95% CI 1.58–3.86) for ECOG 2, compared with ECOG 0 (p for trend < 0.001). title: Adjusted survival curves
text:
Question. The Kaplan-Meier curves by ECOG compare groups that also differ in age and in the proportion of women. What would the curves look like if the three ECOG groups had the same age and sex distribution?
Hazard ratios answer this on the hazard scale; adjusted survival curves answer it on the scale of survival probabilities, which is easier to communicate.

                    factors = vars(sex, ecog), covs = age, adjCurves = TRUE,
                    timeUnit = "months")


The module draws one plot for each factor of the model; covariates such as age get no plot.














Figure 2: Survival by ECOG adjusted for sex and age (solid), with the Kaplan-Meier curves of the same groups (dashed). The caption under the plot lists the variables adjusted for.

title: Adjusted survival curves
text:
How the curves are computed
The module uses direct standardisation (Makuch 1982). For the ECOG 0 curve, it takes every patient in the data, sets their ECOG to 0 while keeping their own sex and age, predicts their survival curve from the Cox model, and averages the 226 curves:
\[\widehat S_{\text{ECOG }0}(t) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \widehat S\bigl(t \mid \text{ECOG } 0,\ \text{sex}_i,\ \text{age}_i\bigr)\]
and the same for ECOG 1 and ECOG 2. The three curves describe the same population (the whole cohort) under three performance statuses, so their differences are due to ECOG alone, as far as the model is right. They are not the curves of the patients who actually had each ECOG; the Kaplan-Meier curves are.

title: Checking proportional hazards
text:
Step 2: the residual plot














Figure 1: Scaled Schoenfeld residuals, one panel per coefficient, against time. Each dot is one death. The dashed red line is the coefficient β of the Cox model (constant by assumption); the blue curve, with its 95% band, is a smooth estimate of how the coefficient changes over time, β(t). The p-value in each title tests that coefficient alone.



How to read it:

The residuals of a factor fall in bands (one per level), so look at the smooth curve, not at the dots.
If the assumption holds, the curve is flat around the dashed line. A curve that rises or falls over time means the effect grows or fades; for a factor, a curve that crosses 0 means the HR crosses 1.
The band is wide where there are few deaths, at the start and especially at the right end. Bends there mean little.

Here the plot shows something the table does not. In roughly the first six months, the curves for both ECOG coefficients rise above the dashed line, and their bands briefly exclude it: the effect of ECOG looks stronger early. This fits the log-log plot of the Kaplan-Meier example, where the ECOG 1 curve starts below ECOG 0 (the very first deaths happened to be in ECOG 0) and overtakes it within a few months. Age shows a similar early wiggle. After that, the curves settle around the dashed lines. For sex the curve drifts upward (towards less protection) late in follow-up, where there are few deaths and the band is wide.
Why do the test and the plot seem to disagree? The test looks for a steady trend of β(t) over the whole follow-up, and a bump in the first months followed by a flat stretch is not a trend. The band is pointwise: over many time points, it will exclude the line somewhere by chance fairly often. The fair reading is: there is no strong evidence against proportional hazards, the single HR for ECOG is a reasonable summary, and there are hints that its effect is largest in the first half-year. A paper about ECOG itself could report that, for example with survival at 6 and 12 months or separate HRs for early and late follow-up (step 3).
The log-log plot of the Kaplan-Meier analysis is the graphical check for one factor at a time without adjustment; the residuals check each coefficient of the adjusted model, including continuous covariates such as age, which the log-log plot cannot handle.

title: Checking proportional hazards
text:
Step 3: if the assumption fails
When a variable clearly violates proportional hazards, there are honest options:

Stratify on it, if you do not need its HR: each level gets its own baseline hazard, and the other HRs are estimated within levels. See step 4.
Report survival at fixed times (Kaplan-Meier or adjusted curves) instead of, or as well as, an HR. These need no proportional-hazards assumption. The restricted mean survival time is another summary that does not (Royston and Parmar 2013).
Split follow-up: estimate one HR for the early period and another for the late period. The cut-off should be chosen on clinical grounds and reported. This, and models with time-varying coefficients, need software beyond this module (for example R’s survival package, which this module uses).
Report the average HR with a clear statement that it averages an effect that changes over time, and show the residual plot. Acceptable when the change is mild.

What not to do: drop the variable because its test was significant, or switch to another test because its p-value is smaller.

title: Survival analysis for prognostic studies
text:
A patient with a new cancer diagnosis asks two questions: will I be cured? and how long do I have? The second one is about time. Prognostic studies follow patients from a starting point (diagnosis, surgery, randomisation) until an event (death, relapse, graft failure) and try to answer it: how likely is the event by one year, by five years, and for which patients is it more likely?
The data from such studies have a peculiarity that breaks the methods you already know: when the study ends, many patients have not had the event yet. We know they survived at least this long, but not how long they will survive. Survival analysis is the set of methods that handles this correctly. This tutorial introduces the three tools you will meet in almost every clinical paper with a time-to-event outcome:
It assumes you know what a p-value, a 95% confidence interval and a 2×2 table are. Each method has a short theory page, then a worked example that you can repeat step by step in jamovi, a free point-and-click statistics program, with the prognosis module. Its menu has the same two entries as this tutorial: Prognosis → Kaplan-Meier and Prognosis → Cox Regression.

text:
Further reading
For a short, readable introduction aimed at clinicians, see the series Survival analysis in the British Journal of Cancer (Clark et al. 2003; Bradburn et al. 2003a, 2003b) and the BMJ statistics notes on the Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test (Bland and Altman 1998, 2004). title: Kaplan-Meier: estimating the survival curve
text:
The probability of surviving two years is the probability of surviving the first year, times the probability of surviving the second year given that you survived the first. The Kaplan-Meier estimator (Kaplan and Meier 1958) applies this idea at every time an event happens. At each event time \(t_j\) it looks only at the \(n_j\) patients still at risk (alive and under observation just before \(t_j\)), counts the \(d_j\) events, and estimates the chance of getting through that moment as \(1 - d_j/n_j\). The survival curve is the product of these factors:
\[\widehat S(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_j}{n_j}\right)\]
Censored patients never contribute a factor. They count in the number at risk up to their censoring time and then leave the risk set. This is how the method uses each patient for exactly as long as they were observed.

title: Kaplan-Meier: estimating the survival curve
text:
How precise is the curve?
Each factor \(1 - d_j/n_j\) is estimated from the patients at risk at that moment, so the curve becomes less precise as that number shrinks. Greenwood’s formula (Greenwood 1926) gives the variance of \(\log \widehat S(t)\) by adding up a contribution from each event time:
\[\widehat{\operatorname{var}}\bigl[\log \widehat S(t)\bigr] = \sum_{t_j \le t} \frac{d_j}{n_j\,(n_j - d_j)}\]
The module (through the R survival package) builds the 95% confidence interval on the log scale and transforms it back:
\[\widehat S(t)\,\exp\Bigl(\pm 1.96\,\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{var}}\bigl[\log \widehat S(t)\bigr]}\Bigr)\]
with an upper limit above 1 cut to 1. The interval is asymmetric and widens quickly when few patients remain at risk, as in the last rows of Table 1. On a plot, the confidence band (option Confidence bands) shows where the curve is still informative. At the right end of a curve, where only a handful of patients are at risk, the steps are large and the band is wide: do not read much into the tail of a Kaplan-Meier curve.

title: Kaplan-Meier: estimating the survival curve
text:
Median survival
The median survival is the first time at which \(\widehat S(t)\) drops to 0.5 or below. It is preferred to the mean because survival times are skewed and the mean cannot be estimated when the curve does not reach 0. Its 95% CI comes from the confidence band: it runs from the time the lower limit of the band crosses 0.5 to the time the upper limit does (Brookmeyer and Crowley 1982). An upper limit can be missing when the band never gets down to 0.5: for the ten patients the median is 12 months, and its 95% CI runs from 6 months to not reached, because the upper limit of the band never falls to 0.5 (Table 1).
If fewer than half of the patients have had the event by the end of follow-up, the median is not reached, and the module leaves the cell empty. That is information, not a failure: report survival at fixed times instead.

title: Kaplan-Meier: estimating the survival curve
text:
Survival at fixed times
“One-year survival 41 %” is \(\widehat S(12)\), read off the curve at 12 months. In the module, type the times in Survival at times (for example 6, 12, 24) and the table gives, for each group and time, the number still at risk, the cumulative number of events, \(\widehat S(t)\) and its CI. These are the numbers clinicians quote, and they need no assumption about the shape of the curve.
A time beyond the last follow-up of a group has 0 patients at risk. The curve is then carried forward from the last observed value, and the module adds a note to the table; those rows are not estimates.

title: Kaplan-Meier: estimating the survival curve
text:
Reading any Kaplan-Meier plot critically

Check the number at risk under the plot (Pocock et al. 2002; Morris et al. 2019). Differences at the right end, with few patients left, are unreliable.
Look at the whole curve, not only the median. Two groups can have the same median and very different early or late survival.
Ask how long patients were followed, and whether losses to follow-up could be informative (see Censoring).
Check the axes. The y-axis should go from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100%); a truncated axis exaggerates differences.

title: Cox regression
text: The log-rank test says whether survival differs between groups. It does not say by how much, it cannot use a continuous variable such as age without cutting it into groups, and it cannot tell whether ECOG predicts survival by itself or only because patients with a worse ECOG are older. Cox regression (Cox 1972) does all three, and is the most used model in clinical research with a time-to-event outcome.

title: Cox regression
text: The log-rank test says whether survival differs between groups. It does not say by how much, it cannot use a continuous variable such as age without cutting it into groups, and it cannot tell whether ECOG predicts survival by itself or only because patients with a worse ECOG are older. Cox regression (Cox 1972) does all three, and is the most used model in clinical research with a time-to-event outcome.

title: Cox regression
text:
The model
Cox regression describes the hazard of a patient with characteristics \(x_1, x_2, \dots\) as a baseline hazard multiplied by a factor that depends on those characteristics:
\[h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\,\exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots)\]

\(h_0(t)\) is the hazard of a patient with all \(x = 0\) (the reference levels). The model makes no assumption about its shape: it can rise, fall or do anything else. This is why the Cox model is called semi-parametric.
For two patients who differ by one unit in \(x_1\) and are equal in everything else, the ratio of their hazards is
\[\mathrm{HR} = \frac{h(t \mid x_1 + 1)}{h(t \mid x_1)} = e^{\beta_1}\]
and it does not depend on \(t\). The model assumes that a variable multiplies the hazard by the same factor at every time: the proportional hazards assumption.

A hazard ratio of 2 means that at any time, among patients still alive, those in one group die at twice the rate of comparable patients in the other group. HR = 1 means no difference; HR < 1 a lower hazard (better prognosis), HR > 1 a higher one.





















Figure 1: Left: group B has twice the hazard of group A at every time, and one HR (2) describes the difference at any time. Right: group B has a high early hazard that falls below A’s later; the survival curves cross, and no single HR describes this.

title: Cox regression
text:
How the model is estimated
Cox’s idea was to avoid estimating \(h_0(t)\) at all. At each time \(t_j\) when a patient dies, ask: of all the patients at risk at that moment (\(R_j\)), what was the probability that it was this patient who died? Under the model it is
\[\frac{e^{\beta^\top x_{(j)}}}{\sum_{i \in R_j} e^{\beta^\top x_i}}\]
The baseline hazard cancels out. Multiplying these probabilities over all event times gives the partial likelihood, and the estimates \(\hat\beta\) are the values that maximise it. Only the order of the event times matters, not their exact values. The standard errors come from the curvature of the likelihood, and the 95% CI of a hazard ratio is \(\exp(\hat\beta \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE})\): asymmetric around the HR.

title: Cox regression
text:
Kinds of variables
Factors (nominal or ordinal variables, in the Factors box) are compared level by level with a reference level: the first level of the variable in jamovi. A factor with \(k\) levels gets \(k - 1\) hazard ratios, each “this level versus the reference”. To change the reference, reorder the levels in the variable’s Setup. For an ordered factor such as ECOG, the option Trend test (p) adds a 1-df test that the hazard changes steadily along the levels, like the trend version of the log-rank test.
Covariates (continuous variables, in the Covariates box) get one hazard ratio per unit increase: per year of age, per mg/dL. The model assumes that each unit multiplies the hazard by the same factor, whether from 40 to 41 years or from 80 to 81 (a log-linear effect); this module does not check that. A per-unit HR can look tiny (1.02 per year) and still matter: over 10 years it is \(1.02^{10} = 1.22\). The option HR for covariates reports it per 1 SD or per any value you choose (for example per 10 years); only the unit changes, not the p-values.

title: Cox regression
text:
Tests

Wald test of each coefficient: \(z = \hat\beta / \mathrm{SE}\); its p-value is in the HR table.
Global tests of the null hypothesis that all HRs in the model are 1: likelihood ratio, Wald and score. They usually agree; the likelihood-ratio test is the most reliable in small samples. With a single factor, the score test is the log-rank test: with the teaching data, sex alone gives a score χ² and a log-rank χ² that agree to three decimals (they are exactly equal when no two deaths happen at the same time).

title: Cox regression
text:
Univariable and multivariable models
A univariable (crude) model has one variable. A multivariable model estimates the effect of each variable adjusted for the others: the HR for ECOG compares patients of the same sex and age. When the two differ, the variable was partly confounded: its crude effect was partly the effect of something associated with it. The option Univariable and multivariable puts both side by side, fitted on the same patients, which is the usual table of a prognostic-factor paper.
How many variables? A classic rule of thumb is about 10 events per estimated coefficient (Peduzzi et al. 1995); it is not a strict limit (Vittinghoff and McCulloch 2007), but with fewer events the estimates become unstable and too extreme. Count events, not patients: 1000 patients with 30 deaths support about three coefficients.

title: Cox regression
text:
Discrimination: the C-index
The concordance index (C-index) (Harrell et al. 1982, 1996) measures how well the model ranks patients: take two patients whose order of events is known; C is the probability that the one the model predicts to be at higher risk has the event first. C = 0.5 is chance and C = 1 perfect ranking. Clinical models with a few variables typically reach 0.6–0.75. C says nothing about calibration (whether the predicted probabilities are right).

title: Cox regression
text:
Proportional hazards
The Cox model assumes that each HR is constant over time. It is violated when, for example, a treatment helps only in the first months, or the curves of two groups cross. Then the single reported HR is a weighted average of different effects at different times, which may describe no patient well (Hernán 2010). Three checks:

Look at the Kaplan-Meier curves. Crossing curves are a warning.
Log-log plot (Kaplan-Meier module): if the hazards are proportional, the curves of \(\log(-\log \widehat S(t))\) against log time are parallel.
Schoenfeld residuals (Schoenfeld 1982; Grambsch and Therneau 1994): at each death, the value of the variable in the patient who died minus the average value in the risk set. Scaled and plotted against time, they show how the coefficient changes over time, \(\beta(t)\). Under proportional hazards \(\beta(t)\) is flat, and the test (option Proportional hazards test) asks whether there is a trend.

A small p-value does not by itself mean the model is useless: in a large study a trivial change in the HR gives a small p, and in a small study a real change can be missed (Stensrud and Hernán 2020). Always look at the residual plot. The assumptions example shows what to do when the assumption fails.

Stratification
A variable that violates proportional hazards, or one you need to adjust for but not to estimate (for example the hospital in a multicentre study), can go into Strata. The model then gets a separate baseline hazard \(h_{0s}(t)\) for each stratum, with shapes free to differ, while the HRs of the other variables are shared across strata. The price is that there is no HR for the stratification variable.

title: Cox regression
text:
Interactions
Sometimes the effect of one variable depends on another: a marker is prognostic in women but not in men, or a treatment works only in early stages. This is effect modification, tested by adding an interaction term (Interactions section of the Cox panel). The likelihood-ratio test for the interaction tells whether the effect differs between subgroups; the table Hazard ratios within subgroups gives the effect in each one.
Two warnings. With an interaction in the model, the “main effect” HR of a variable applies only at the reference level of the other variable. And the power to detect an interaction is low: finding a significant effect in one subgroup and not in another is not evidence that the effects differ; only the interaction test is. The interactions example shows both.

title: Cox regression
text:
Adjusted survival curves
Hazard ratios are hard to translate into probabilities. Adjusted survival curves show what survival would look like in each group of a factor if all groups had the same distribution of the other variables. The module uses direct standardisation (Makuch 1982): for each level of the factor, it predicts the survival curve of every patient in the data as if they had that level (keeping their own values of the other variables), and averages these curves. Comparing them with the unadjusted Kaplan-Meier curves shows how much of the difference between groups is explained by the other variables. Adjusted curves are not available for stratified models.






ImportantWhat a hazard ratio is not




Not a risk ratio. HR = 0.5 does not mean “half as many deaths at 1 year”. The difference in the probability of death depends on the baseline risk and on the time horizon; report survival probabilities (Kaplan-Meier or adjusted curves) as well.
Not a ratio of median survival times, except under special assumptions.
Not constant in reality just because the model says so: check it.

title: Glossary
text:
Adjusted survival curve

The survival curve each group would have if all groups had the same distribution of the other variables of a Cox model; the module computes it by direct standardisation. Adjusted curves

At risk

A patient is at risk at time \(t\) if they are alive (event-free) and still under observation just before \(t\). The number at risk \(n_j\) is the denominator of each Kaplan-Meier step. Kaplan-Meier

Baseline hazard, \(h_0(t)\)

The hazard of a patient with all variables at their reference level (or 0) in a Cox model. Its shape is not estimated as part of the hazard ratios. Cox

C-index (concordance)

The probability that, of two patients whose order of events is known, the one the model predicts to be at higher risk has the event first. 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect. Cox

Censoring (right censoring)

Observation of a patient ends before the event: their survival time is known to be longer than the observed time. Administrative censoring happens when the study closes; informative censoring, when the reason for censoring is related to prognosis, biases the estimates. Censoring

Competing risk

An event that prevents the event of interest (death from another cause when the event is death from cancer). Treating it as censoring overestimates the cumulative incidence. Kaplan-Meier

Confounding

A distortion of the association between a variable and the outcome because of a third variable associated with both. In the tutorial, part of the crude effect of age was due to ECOG. Cox example

Cox regression (proportional hazards model)

\(h(t \mid x) = h_0(t)\exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \dots)\): a regression model for the hazard, which gives hazard ratios adjusted for the other variables. Cox

Cumulative hazard, \(H(t)\)

The hazard added up from 0 to \(t\); \(S(t) = e^{-H(t)}\). Time-to-event data

Cumulative incidence

The probability of having had the event by time \(t\), \(1 - S(t)\) when there are no competing risks.

Direct standardisation

Averaging the predicted survival curves of all patients after setting the variable of interest to the same level for everyone; used for adjusted survival curves.

Effect modification (interaction)

The effect of one variable depends on the value of another. Tested with an interaction term in a Cox model. Interactions

Event

What ends the survival time: death, relapse, progression. Its definition, and the time origin, must be stated.

Events per variable

The number of events divided by the number of coefficients of a model; roughly 10 or more is a common rule of thumb. Cox

Greenwood’s formula

The variance of the Kaplan-Meier estimate, used for its confidence interval. Kaplan-Meier

Hazard, \(h(t)\)

The rate of the event at time \(t\) among patients still event-free just before \(t\); a rate, with units (per month), not a probability. Time-to-event data

Hazard ratio (HR)

The ratio of the hazards of two groups (or per unit of a covariate). HR = 1: no difference; HR < 1: lower hazard. It is not a risk ratio. Cox

Kaplan-Meier estimator

The product of the conditional probabilities of surviving each event time, \(\prod (1 - d_j/n_j)\); the standard estimate of the survival curve. Kaplan-Meier

Log-log plot

\(\log(-\log \widehat S(t))\) against log time, by group; parallel curves support proportional hazards. Assumptions

Log-rank test

Compares survival curves by adding up observed minus expected events at each event time. Weighted versions: Gehan-Breslow, Tarone-Ware, Peto-Peto. Log-rank

Median follow-up

The median time patients were (or would have been) followed, estimated with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method: the event and censoring indicators are swapped. KM example

Median survival

The first time at which the Kaplan-Meier curve reaches 0.5 or less. “Not reached” if fewer than half of the patients had the event. Kaplan-Meier

Partial likelihood

The likelihood that the Cox model maximises: at each event time, the probability that the patient who died was the one to die among those at risk. The baseline hazard cancels out.

Proportional hazards

The assumption of the Cox model that each hazard ratio is constant over time. Assumptions

Reference level

The level of a factor that the others are compared with (HR = 1); in jamovi, the first level of the variable.

Schoenfeld residuals

For each death, the variable’s value in the patient who died minus its average in the risk set; plotted against time, they show whether a coefficient changes over time. Assumptions

Stratified Cox model

A Cox model with a separate baseline hazard in each stratum and common hazard ratios; the stratification variable gets no HR. Assumptions

Survival function, \(S(t)\)

The probability of being event-free beyond time \(t\), \(P(T > t)\).

Trend test

A 1-df test that survival (or the hazard) changes steadily along the levels of an ordered factor. Log-rank

Univariable and multivariable

A univariable (crude) model has one variable; a multivariable model estimates each variable’s effect adjusted for the others.

Wald, likelihood ratio and score tests

Three ways of testing coefficients of a Cox model; the global versions test that all hazard ratios are 1. With one factor, the score test is the log-rank test.
